title: Thirteen Athletes Qualified in a Single Day. The Triple Jumpers Were the Story India Didn't See Coming.
excerpt: Six of the top six men's triple jumpers all cleared the Asian Games mark at Bhubaneswar — Praveen Chithravel led with a 16.92m opener — as Day 3 of the Inter-State Championships showed just how deep India's track and field talent pool has become
body:
The numbers from Day 1 and Day 2 in Bhubaneswar were already hard to ignore. Jyothi Yarraji slipped back under 13 seconds in the 100-metre hurdles. Anushka Yadav rewrote the national record in hammer throw — twice in 40 minutes. Dev Meena cleared 5.46 metres in the pole vault to claim the national record outright.

Then came Day 3, and the 65th National Inter-State Senior Athletics Championships showed that the depth ran deeper than anyone had counted on.

Thirteen athletes cleared Asian Games qualifying standards across five events on a single evening at the Kalinga Stadium on Friday. The headline belonged to the triple jump pit, where something unprecedented happened: all six of the top finishers surpassed the 16.28-metre mark that the Athletics Federation of India has set for selection to the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya.

**The Triple Jump Breakthrough**

Praveen Chithravel, the 22-year-old national record holder ranked 19th in the world, set the tone with an opening effort of 16.92 metres to take gold. It was a statement jump — delivered first round, with no warm-up attempt — from an athlete who has been steadily climbing the global rankings since winning Youth Olympic silver in Buenos Aires as a teenager.

Behind him, Karthik U (16.80m) and Selva Prabhu (16.79m) pushed past the qualifying standard with room to spare. And the extraordinary part: positions four, five, and six all cleared 16.28m as well. Indian men's triple jump has never had this kind of depth. Two years ago, clearing the qualifying mark was a story in itself. On Friday, *not* clearing it was the exception.

The AFI selection committee will name two athletes for the Asian Games squad once the championships conclude. The difficulty of that choice — with six credible candidates — is itself a marker of how far the event has come in India.

**Hammer and Discus — Power on Display**

The field events started with the men's hammer throw. Damneet Singh of Punjab opened the evening session with a winning heave of 69.72 metres, sailing past the qualifying mark of 69.12m. Rajasthan's Praveen Kumar was right behind at 69.58m, giving India two hammer throwers clearly above the Asian Games standard.

Over at the discus circle, Haryana owned the podium. Seema threw 59.73 metres for gold, Sanya Yadav took silver with 56.05m, and Nidhi claimed bronze at 55.92m — all three clearing the 55.48-metre qualification mark. A clean sweep from a single state, in an event where India has traditionally struggled for international depth, said as much about Haryana's athletics infrastructure as it did about the individual throwers.

**Speed Over Barriers**

On the track, Tejas Shirse confirmed his status as India's premier hurdler with a comfortable victory in the 110-metre hurdles. His winning time of 13.61 seconds dipped under the Asian Games qualifying time of 13.63 — not by a dramatic margin, but enough to underline his consistency. Shirse, the national record holder, represented India at the 2025 World Championships in Tokyo and will be a strong medal contender in Japan.

In the women's 400-metre hurdles heats, Tamil Nadu's Vithya Ramraj clocked 56.69 seconds, keeping her on track for an Asian Games berth as the competition progresses into its final days.

**The Bigger Picture**

This championships is the last major domestic trial before the AFI selects India's contingent for the Asian Games. The numbers across three days tell a story of a programme that is producing results at a pace Indian athletics has rarely seen.

National records have fallen in hammer throw, pole vault, and hurdles. Asian Games qualifying standards have been met in everything from sprints to throws. And in the triple jump, India now has half a dozen athletes who can compete at the continental level — a scenario that would have seemed far-fetched even two seasons ago.

For Indian diaspora sports fans who grew up watching the country struggle for depth outside cricket, the transformation is worth paying attention to. India sent its largest-ever track and field contingent to the 2025 World Championships. The Bhubaneswar meet suggests the squad headed to Aichi-Nagoya could be even stronger.

The championships continue through Saturday, with finals in several sprint events and the decathlon expected to produce more qualifying marks. If the first three days are any guide, the AFI selectors will have more difficult decisions to make — the kind of difficulty any federation should welcome.
